video_title: Central Banks Are Losing Control | Ideas Lab | Ep.50
gist: Economist Manoj Pradhan (Talking Heads Macro, co-author with Charles Goodhart of 'The Unanchored Central Banker') argues the demographic sweet spot that delivered three decades of falling goods inflation is over, and that government dis-saving from aging populations — not household saving — will dominate and push real interest rates structurally higher. His core investable claim: in economies with 100-140% debt-to-GDP, central banks can no longer single-mindedly fight inflation, so bond-market/fiscal stability will take precedence and the inflation target will slip, with advanced economies increasingly disciplined like emerging markets (Brazil, Truss-era UK) rather than exempt from it.

themes.theme: The demographic sweet spot and its reversal

insights.claim: Pradhan attributes the 1990s-2010s disinflation to three simultaneous labor-supply forces — baby boomers entering work, women's rising participation, and China's integration — which lowered goods inflation, wages, nominal rates and, by shifting desired capital out of the West, the equilibrium real rate as well.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: If the disinflation was supply-driven rather than policy-driven, the reversal of those same forces removes the structural bid for duration and argues against a return to the pre-2020 rate regime.
insights.quote: you were able to bring down not only the cost of producing goods, um goods inflation, wages, uh and therefore nominal interest rates, but also the real interest rate because ex ante investment falls relative to savings in the west

insights.claim: Central bank independence was politically cheap during the demographic sweet spot because falling inflation and rates helped incumbent governments get reelected; Pradhan implies independence was granted conditionally and can be withdrawn when the tailwind disappears.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: Frames central bank independence as a cyclical political bargain rather than an institutional constant — a key premise for pricing long-term inflation risk premia.
insights.quote: because central banks were able to help generate an environment in which the incumbent government found it easy to get reelected. The governments themselves were more than willing to give central banks as much independence as they needed.

insights.claim: China's labor supply is now dwindling to the point that Chinese cities compete with each other for the next round of migrant workers, and economists are debating whether China has hit the Lewis point — the level at which further migration damages the economy.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: The single largest historical source of global labor-cost deflation is exhausted; China can no longer export disinflation to the same degree.
insights.quote: China's labor supply is now dwindling to the extent that cities within China themselves are in intense competition for the next round of migrant workers

insights.claim: The post-pandemic surge in immigration was a worldwide, unanticipated positive labor-supply shock that has now triggered social and political backlash almost everywhere, so external labor supply will be structurally weak for the foreseeable future.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: Removes the main release valve for labor shortages, supporting persistent wage and services-inflation pressure in advanced economies.
insights.quote: It's very difficult to think that the change in the atmosphere surrounding immigration is going to change in the foreseeable future, which means external labor supply itself is going to be weak.

insights.claim: With the exception of a handful of economies including parts of sub-Saharan Africa, most countries are now below the 2.1 replacement fertility rate, and India — above replacement at the national level four years ago — has now fallen below it too.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan and host Kevin Coldiron
insights.so_what: The labor-shortage thesis is now global rather than confined to Japan and Europe, extending the higher-real-rate argument to emerging markets.
insights.quote: most economies have fallen so sharply below that it would take a real change in social, economic, and political conditions to get that up

insights.claim: Pronatalist policy has repeatedly failed — Hungary's program, China's recent large support package for young families, and Norway's near-equal paternity leave have not reversed fertility declines — so Pradhan sees getting birth rates back above 2.1 as incredibly difficult.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: Closes off the main optimistic offset to the demographic thesis; investors should not underwrite a fertility rebound in long-horizon models.
insights.quote: Maybe a possible modest improvement, but something that gets them above 2.1 looks incredibly difficult to me.

insights.claim: The dominant reason young families cite for having fewer or no children is the cost of raising them, per a chart in Pradhan and Goodhart's book from Garuso and Spears and the UNHCR fertility report — meaning fertility is an economic rather than purely cultural variable.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: Implies fertility responds to affordability, which is itself worsened by the higher-rate, higher-housing-cost world the thesis predicts — a self-reinforcing loop.

themes.theme: Blind spots in conventional real-rate models

insights.claim: Pradhan accepts the consensus logic that longer life expectancy raises household saving and depresses real rates, but argues it ignores that government dis-saving from pensions and elderly healthcare will rise even faster, so the net effect is a dis-saving economy and higher real rates.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: The central rebuttal to the 'aging is deflationary / secular stagnation' trade — argues structurally short duration rather than long.
insights.quote: And so, if you're a dis-saving economy, it's very, very, very hard to think that real interest rates will remain subdued. Just very difficult.

insights.claim: Pradhan says mainstream models still fail to incorporate the cost of healthcare and elderly care because Western economies have not yet reached a critical mass of elderly people, and points to Japan, China and Scandinavia as the leading indicators of how large that cost becomes.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: Suggests consensus fiscal projections are systematically too optimistic; healthcare-cost inflation is an under-priced macro variable.

insights.claim: Housing is the second under-modeled channel to higher real rates: population growth is the primary driver of home demand, and continued construction plus continued housing demand puts upward pressure on real rates.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: Argues housing investment competes for scarce savings rather than being purely rate-sensitive demand — relevant for homebuilders and mortgage spreads.

insights.claim: Aging reduces the fungibility of the existing housing stock from old to young because elderly people are far less willing to move, so new family formation requires newly built homes rather than turnover of existing ones.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: Undercuts the common assumption that boomer downsizing will release supply and cool house prices; supports persistent construction demand.
insights.quote: the the the fungibility of housing from the old to the young falls as a society becomes increasingly aged, which means new family formation depends on new homes being created

insights.claim: In rapidly aging economies such as Italy, Japan and China, rural populations and rural homes are dwindling fast — Italian mayors offering homes for a euro — so urban infrastructure must be built out as if the whole economy were still growing even when it isn't.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: National population decline can coexist with rising urban capex needs — a reason aggregate demographic decline does not automatically mean falling investment demand.
insights.quote: In many economies that are rapidly aging, I mean I can think of Italy for one, Japan for another, China as a third, rural populations and rural homes are dwindling very very very quickly.

insights.claim: Pradhan says the standard modeling shortcut of holding government deficits, debt and pensions at a fixed proportion of GDP invalidates the results, because the link from aging to fiscal outcomes is more powerful and complicated than the link to household savings.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: A concrete reason to discount institutional r-star estimates that use these assumptions when setting long-run terminal-rate expectations.
insights.quote: making assumptions that government deficits, debts, and pension are a fixed proportion of GDP just does not work

themes.theme: AI: labor demand, inequality and the rate channel

insights.claim: Pradhan's non-consensus point on an AI labor collapse is that the hard problem is not agreeing on universal basic income but financing it — taxing society as a whole would never be politically viable, so the tax would have to be directed at companies that cut workforces while maintaining profitability or raising profit share.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: Identifies visible labor-replacement plus rising profit share as the political trigger for targeted corporate taxation — an under-priced policy risk in the exact names investors crowd into.
insights.quote: if you decide to uh, provide a universal basic income for workers, you cannot finance that by taxing society as a whole. Politically, it would never fly.

insights.claim: The second-order conclusion is contrarian for equities: the large investments people make in companies expected to replace labor will not pay off as expected precisely in the scenario of a catastrophic decline in labor demand, because that scenario forces confiscatory taxation of those same companies.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: The AI-displacement trade is self-defeating in its own bull-tail case — a reason to hedge policy risk rather than simply own the labor-replacement basket.
insights.quote: this huge investment that people make in companies where they believe uh, labor is just going to collapse is not the way things will turn out for the stock market if you get a real catastrophic decline in labor demand

insights.claim: Following David Autor, Pradhan argues past technology shocks hit manufacturing, which is concentrated by region or sector (Sheffield steel, Detroit cars) and produced mass localized unemployment, whereas the AI shock hits services that exist everywhere — an accountant in every small town and corporate entity — so cutting 20-30% of accounting work spreads the shock thinly enough to be absorbed.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: Argues against a concentrated AI unemployment crisis, which weakens the disinflationary-AI narrative and supports his tight-labor-market inflation call.
insights.quote: There's an accountant in every small town, every village, every corporate entity that exists, whether they're small, medium, or large.

insights.claim: Pradhan's mechanism for AI being net job-creating is redeployment: a company cutting 20% of accounting costs redirects that spend to core activities — the same pattern as China's manufacturing shock, where US manufacturing employment fell sharply but employment elsewhere rose substantially more as inflation and rates fell.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: If AI raises rather than lowers aggregate employment, it fails to relieve the labor shortage and therefore fails to offset the inflation impulse.

insights.claim: Pradhan calls it his most controversial claim that AI will reduce inequality if you exclude the top 0.2-0.5% who get very rich, because it lowers barriers to entry into higher-paid service professions and lets young companies and emerging markets do well.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: Directly opposes the consensus that AI concentrates returns — and if right, favors EM and small-cap/young-company exposure over incumbent concentration.
insights.quote: if you look at it as an 80/20, there's a good chance that inequality actually falls. It allows young companies to do very well. It allows emerging markets to do very well.

insights.claim: Pradhan links AI to rates via a Jackson Hole paper by Mian, Straub and Sufi showing higher inequality means lower interest rates because the rich save more and those savings flow into financial markets; if AI lowers inequality, those flows shrink and interest rates get pulled higher.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: A rarely-made transmission channel from AI to the long end — bearish bonds through a route unrelated to growth or productivity.
insights.quote: the higher the inequality in the economy, the lower interest rates tend to be

insights.claim: Hyperscaler capital spending has breached $700 billion this year and, unlike the credit-financed internet buildout of the 2000s, is funded largely from cash — which converts money-market-fund balances that were supplying loanable funds into physical capex and creates a dual headwind for interest rates.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: Explains why the AI capex cycle is rate-positive even without leverage — and why the 'no credit risk this time' comfort misses the funding-market drain.
insights.quote: if you take 700 billion dollars of cash that was resting in a money market mutual fund and now use it for capex, you're almost creating a dual headwind for interest rates

insights.claim: Pradhan sizes the combined shock to the loanable-funds market this year at roughly $1.3 trillion: $700 billion of hyperscaler capex plus the CRFB estimate that the one big beautiful bill adds $600 billion to this year's deficit.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: A quantified, dated case for higher real yields this year — the cleanest tradable number in the episode.
insights.quote: So you're seeing a net change in the demand for funds by about 1.3 trillion dollars this year. That's got to have an increase in real interest rates.

insights.claim: AI's electricity demand and the resulting data center buildout are an inflationary cost channel visible across emerging markets, Ireland and parts of the US, and face social opposition — so AI is not a frictionless offset to labor scarcity.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: Power costs and siting opposition are a live inflation and execution risk for the AI capex cycle, not just a utilities growth story.
insights.quote: the the demand for electricity from AI is clearly going to be a story that changes, hence the demand for data centers and the like, to which there's social opposition

insights.claim: Pradhan reports using Claude heavily in his own research workflow — the first edit pass of the book was run with Claude and it built his multi-country fiscal policy simulator — with data validation taking him twenty times longer than the model took to build the tool.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: A working macro economist's data point that the binding constraint in AI-assisted analysis has shifted from code generation to data verification.
insights.quote: In fact, it took me 20 times more to make sure the data was right than it took Claude to build the simulator.

themes.theme: Fiscal fixes: older workers and child-linked taxation

insights.claim: Pradhan's most easily implementable fiscal proposal is tax incentives for firms to hire workers over 55, graded by how cognitive the sector is — since experience and judgment compound in cognitive work while physical roles cannot be incentivized the same way.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: A cheap, politically viable lever that would partially relieve labor scarcity — watch for it appearing in budgets as the labor shortage bites.
insights.quote: I think not only could you provide an incentive for firms to hire older workers, you could give them a graded incentive depending on how cognitive of a particular sector is.

insights.claim: Pradhan pairs hiring incentives with a flexible retirement age in which people who keep working have their pension entitlement rolled over at the going interest rate, giving them both labor income and accrued pension income later.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: Extends effective labor supply without cutting benefits outright — the least politically painful fiscal repair on the table.

insights.claim: Pradhan says AI has already reduced demand for young workers because firms implicitly finance part of a new graduate's education while they build human capital, so hiring incentives should extend to fresh college graduates as well as older workers.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: Entry-level hiring is the first visible AI labor effect; graduate unemployment is a leading indicator to watch, and a subsidy target.
insights.quote: That's one of the problems that AI has generated, right? And on the one hand when you look at young young people, the the reason that there's less demand for them is while they're picking up human capital, um the company is implicitly financing some of the education.

insights.claim: Pradhan proposes a purely positive-economics differential tax rate on people who choose not to have children, ring-fenced so the pool can only fund their own retirement health insurance and held in escrow and repaid if they later do have children.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: A concrete template for how governments may reallocate the elderly-care burden — controversial and hard to implement, but a signal of the direction of fiscal creativity under demographic strain.
insights.quote: That pool of taxes cannot be used for anything else except paying for health insurance for your own retirement into the future.

insights.claim: The book finds that around 80% of elderly care is provided within the family, which means childlessness shifts that labor-intensive burden onto the state or for-profit providers — and the UK has stopped hiring foreign workers for healthcare and caring roles just as the burden rises.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: Quantifies the hidden, unpriced share of eldercare about to be monetized onto public budgets — bullish structural demand for paid care and bearish for fiscal balances.
insights.quote: If 80% of elderly care comes from within the family, not having one child or having any children changes that dynamic dramatically.

insights.claim: Pradhan says the non-discretionary part of budgets — predominantly healthcare — is the piece that must be cut, but that it cannot be done until there is either a way to please the population or an efficient AI- and robotics-led version of healthcare delivery.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: Makes healthcare automation the pivotal variable for fiscal sustainability — a long-horizon thematic with macro-level payoff, not just sector upside.
insights.quote: we all know that the non-discretionary part of budgets, which is predominantly health care, has to be somehow reduced. But until you find a way to please the population or an efficient AI robotics-led version of health care, it's very hard to do.

themes.theme: The two Phillips curves: goods vs services inflation

insights.claim: Pradhan splits the Phillips curve in two: a domestic services curve driven by labor-market slack and wages, and a goods curve which since the 1990s has had little to do with domestic economies and is set primarily in China and in China-linked commodity prices.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: Means domestic output gaps are the wrong input for forecasting headline inflation — and that China's price cycle is the dominant exogenous variable.
insights.quote: the traditional discussion around the Phillips curve... needs to be split into because there's one part for goods and there's one part for services

insights.claim: Pradhan's charts show the vast majority of economies saw inflation fall since the 1990s because goods inflation fell — either during China's benign low-cost manufacturing period or its malign period when housing collapsed — implying central banks did very little to earn the disinflation they were credited with.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: If the inflation-targeting track record was borrowed from China, central bank credibility is far more fragile than markets assume when the borrowing stops.
insights.quote: And so, central banks have really had to do very little. They've been able to keep their economies and domestically generated inflation quite steady and just reap a lot of the benefits of having falling goods inflation.

insights.claim: Pradhan predicts future inflation will be determined by services inflation tied to labor markets, with more government spending keeping labor markets still tighter and services inflation elevated.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: Argues for a persistently higher inflation floor that is sticky and domestically generated — harder for central banks to look through than goods shocks.
insights.quote: We believe that the future holds whatever is going to happen to services inflation, and that's tied to labor markets.

insights.claim: Pradhan notes that even Germany, the archetypal manufacturing economy, derives only about 20% of value added from manufacturing and 80% from services — underlining that advanced economies are services economies whose domestic inflation is wage-driven.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: Calibrates how little of advanced-economy inflation can be imported-disinflated away, reinforcing the sticky-services-inflation call.
insights.quote: Germany has a 20% share of value added from manufacturing. Still 80% from services.

insights.claim: Pradhan argues Volcker could deliver two sharp recessions by raising rates to the moon only because there was very little debt in the economy, so hiking hurt activity without threatening fiscal stability — a precondition that no longer exists.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: Kills the 'a modern Volcker moment could always fix inflation' backstop that underpins long-end demand.
insights.quote: He was able to do that because there was very little debt in the economy at that time. So, when you raise the interest rates, there were repercussions for the economy, but not for fiscal stability.

insights.claim: At 100% debt-to-GDP, Pradhan says double-digit policy rates would succeed in creating a recession and lowering inflation today but would blow out deficits so much that the resulting debt would have to be inflated away later — making aggressive disinflation self-defeating.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: Implies any successful tightening cycle now plants the seeds of the next inflation — argues for structurally higher breakevens and inflation-linked exposure.
insights.quote: in order to dissolve that debt into the future, you'll have to generate inflation in the future

insights.claim: Pradhan's central conclusion is that a central banker in a highly indebted society can no longer single-mindedly pursue inflation and must trade off inflation-fighting against fiscal instability — and both he and the host agree bond-market stability will take precedence, so the inflation objective slips.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan and Kevin Coldiron
insights.so_what: The core trade: expect inflation to run above target persistently while policy prioritizes funding costs — steepeners, real assets, and inflation protection.
insights.quote: You will have to take some choice between fighting inflation and balancing off fiscal instability.

insights.claim: Pradhan flags central bank balance sheet size as a huge open question under the incoming chair Walsh, alongside the level of interest rates and how central banks conceptualize inflation.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: A specific, near-dated catalyst: balance sheet policy under a new chair is where the fiscal-monetary trade-off will show up first.
insights.quote: but also for the size of balance sheets, which is a huge question with the incoming chair Walsh

insights.claim: Pradhan uses the QE-to-QE-infinity sequence as evidence that once a policy tool is introduced for a problem that does not go away, markets make its repeated use inevitable.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: Reusable rule for pricing policy path: expect emergency tools to be redeployed, and price the option accordingly rather than treating them as one-offs.
insights.quote: once you introduce a particular tool to solve a particular problem, if that problem doesn't go away, the market almost makes it inevitable that that tool will be used again

insights.claim: Pradhan expects US fiscal spending to exceed CBO projections because the bulk of the one big beautiful bill's cuts arrive a couple of years out and Social Security's reserve fund faces a fiscal cliff around 2033, which no candidate in the early 2030s will politically allow to hit.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: Gives a dated fiscal catalyst (2033) and a reason to treat official deficit baselines as a floor, not a forecast.
insights.quote: Social security through its reserve fund faces a fiscal cliff around 2033. It's very difficult to think of the next presidential candidate or whoever is coming in in the early 2030s who's going to allow that to happen because that is a catastrophic political calculus.

insights.claim: Pradhan argues that rather than accepting austerity, governments facing high borrowing costs can respond with financial repression or by pressuring central banks into cutting rates to reduce interest expense — so the self-correcting mechanism may be political rather than market-driven.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: Financial repression is the tail investors should hedge: capped nominal yields with uncapped inflation is the worst outcome for nominal bonds.
insights.quote: The government can react too... by instituting financial repression or by forcing central banks to with not be able to withstand political pressure and reduce interest rates thereby reducing their interest expenses.

insights.claim: Pradhan does not expect an orderly transition — he says it is very difficult to change a government's perspective until there is a crisis, small or big, and unrealistic to think the adjustment happens smoothly without a real shock to governments.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: Argues the regime change arrives as a discrete event rather than a gradual repricing — favors owning convexity/tail hedges over linear positioning.
insights.quote: it's unrealistic to think that this will happen in a smooth way without a real shock to governments

themes.theme: Emerging-market-style bond discipline arrives in developed markets

insights.claim: Pradhan reads the Truss administration episode, France's experience, the reaction to Japan's new administration and the reaction to higher US fiscal spending as evidence that the era of advanced economies receiving different bond-market treatment than emerging markets is close to ending.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: Argues for widening term premia and event risk around DM budget announcements — trade DM fiscal events the way you would trade EM ones.
insights.quote: the days in which advanced economies were given a different treatment than emerging market economies are probably close to coming to an end

insights.claim: Brazil is Pradhan's live template for the debt trap: its primary deficit — the new spending — is under half a percent of GDP and compliant with its fiscal rule, yet the headline deficit is 8-9% of GDP because almost all the rest is interest cost created after the central bank cut rates too quickly and let inflation rise.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: The cleanest existing case study of a central bank policy error becoming a permanent fiscal problem — the specific failure mode to watch for in DM cutting cycles.
insights.quote: The entire rest of the 8 and 9% fiscal deficit is which is in there, comes from really high interest rates.

insights.claim: Pradhan is not forecasting Brazil-style 14-15% policy rates for advanced economies, but argues that with 100%, 120% and 140% debt-to-GDP ratios, a rise of just two or three percentage points in rates makes a huge difference to the fiscal outcome.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: Sets the actual threshold for the debt-spiral trade — a modest, plausible rate move, not a tail scenario.
insights.quote: for the advanced economies with 100 and 120 and 140% debt-to-GDP ratios, raising interest rates by two or three percentage points makes a huge difference in what the outcome's going to be

insights.claim: In the UK, the OBR's assessed fiscal headroom rose from about 7 billion pounds to 22 billion pounds under the Labour administration, but Pradhan says the market's willingness to believe a high-spending, high-revenue budget is financed by growth has been short-lived because the growth has not materialized.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: Headroom metrics are a weak anchor for gilt confidence; the growth assumption is the real variable to track in UK fiscal events.
insights.quote: the markets' willingness to believe that that budget has been financed adequately by growth and by fiscal revenues has been really short-lived

insights.claim: Pradhan cites South Africa as a rare case of monetary dominance in a highly indebted economy: by de facto choosing a lower inflation target, the South African Reserve Bank cut about 1.5% of nominal growth out of fiscal projections and thereby forced the government to be far more austere.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: Shows the mechanism by which a central bank can still impose fiscal discipline — a template and a screen for which sovereigns escape the unanchoring.
insights.quote: The South African Reserve Bank, by choosing a lower inflation target de facto, has cut out 1 and 1/2% of nominal growth from fiscal projections, thereby forcing the government to be far more austere.

insights.claim: New Zealand's administration is focused on raising a primary surplus in anticipation of the coming demographic and fiscal challenges, but Pradhan stresses that South Africa and New Zealand are exceptions rather than the rule.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: A short list of sovereigns whose fiscal path may diverge favourably — potential relative-value longs against the unanchored majority.
insights.quote: These things These things can happen, and they do happen, but they are more the exception than the rule.

insights.claim: Pradhan partially accepts the self-correcting argument that yields above roughly 5% would trigger a funding crisis and forced deleveraging, but says there are limits to how long markets will believe fiscal claims and that governments will intervene before the market completes the correction.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan responding to Kevin Coldiron
insights.so_what: Means the deflationary-bust hedge is real but likely truncated by policy intervention — position for policy response rather than a clean deflation trade.
insights.quote: No, I think I think they have some validity.

insights.claim: Pradhan says governments must also resist spending more as elections approach, and openly doubts they will — adding that if the central bank cannot deliver lower rates, politicians will fall back on pressuring it as a crutch.
insights.speaker: Manoj Pradhan
insights.so_what: Ties the electoral calendar directly to central bank independence risk — a recurring, schedulable source of policy-credibility repricing.
insights.quote: Second is you have to avoid the temptation to spend more money when it's getting when it's getting closer to election time. Good luck with that.
